title: Devlens Research Summary: Power and gas cuts stall Bangladesh's factories
excerpt: The first BIDS-BCI Industry 100 survey finds output flat, grid outages doubled to 4.1 hours a day, machinery investment collapsed and hiring down 19%.
content:
Bangladesh's medium and large factories made no more goods in April to June 2026 than in an average quarter of 2025, and they cut spending on machinery almost to nothing. A new survey by the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies (BIDS) and the Bangladesh Chamber of Industries (BCI) puts the blame mainly on power and gas cuts. This summary sets out what the survey found and what it means for jobs, workers and the organisations that support them.

The source

The BIDS-BCI Industry 100 is a new quarterly survey of medium and large manufacturers. Its first round was presented at BIDS in Agargaon on Tuesday, 24 November, by BIDS research director Kazi Iqbal, with State Minister for Planning Zonayed Abdur Rahim Saki and BCI president Anwar-ul Alam Chowdhury present. BIDS director general AK Enamul Haque chaired the event.

Data were collected from 130 factories in 14 sub-sectors, which together produce about 90% of the output of medium and large industry. The plan is to keep a permanent sample of 100 factories. Each round compares the latest quarter with the average quarter of 2025, and results are weighted by each sector's share of production. The survey tracks four areas separately: production, inputs, employment and business sentiment. The second round, for July to September, is under way.

Finding 1: output stalled

Real manufacturing output was 0.4% lower in April to June than the 2025 quarterly average. The average hides wide differences. Forty factories raised real output by more than 5%, while 30 reported a fall of more than 5%.

Textiles were hit hardest. Their real output fell 20% and capacity use dropped from 73% to 55%. Ready-made garments did better, with real output up 2% and capacity use up from 68% to 70%. Across all factories, capacity use slipped from 67% to 66%, and the number working at less than half capacity rose from 19 to 28.

Finding 2: power and gas cuts doubled and quadrupled

Of the 128 factories on grid electricity, 116 reported longer outages than in 2025. Average grid disruption doubled to 4.1 hours a day. Among factories on piped gas, disruption almost quadrupled, from 0.9 to 3.2 hours a day.

Only 7% of factories were satisfied with grid power quality, down from 38% in 2025. Satisfaction with gas supply fell from 70% to 17%. About four in five factories (79%) named power and energy as their biggest obstacle.

Finding 3: costs rose and investment collapsed

Average quarterly energy spending per factory rose 5%, to Tk 3.32 crore. Within that, electricity spending rose 8%, generator fuel 15% and LPG 25%, as factories paid more to run their own back-up. Gas spending fell 4%, which fits with less gas being delivered. Freight, the largest operating cost, rose 10%, and 94% of factories reported higher raw material costs, according to The Business Standard.

The sharpest change was in investment. Average quarterly spending on capital machinery per factory fell from Tk 1.76 crore in 2025 to Tk 11 lakh. Machinery purchases fell in every sector except pharmaceuticals and chemicals.

Finding 4: fewer jobs, fewer new hires

Employment across the 130 factories fell 1%, from 137,100 to 135,700 workers. New hires per factory fell 19%, and so did departures. The Business Standard reported that most hiring was to fill posts left by workers who quit, suggesting factories were holding on to staff rather than creating new jobs.

All five measures of current business conditions scored between 36 and 43, below the no-change mark of 50. Expectations for July to September were less gloomy, at 49 to 54. The expected production index stood at 54.

How this compares with official figures

The survey differs from some official indicators. The Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics large-scale manufacturing index rose 11% year on year in April to June, and merchandise exports rose 13.7% in dollar terms. BIDS noted that April to June 2025 was a weak quarter with two Eid closures, which flatters the year-on-year comparison. Against the average quarter of 2025, the BBS index fell 2.1%, which is closer to the survey's result.

The survey comes ten days after a GDP forensic audit presented at BBS on 14 November found that GDP growth had been overstated by an average of 0.7 to 1.3 percentage points a year since 2014-15, and that about 41% of the overstated growth between 2014-15 and 2018-19 came from manufacturing, according to The Business Standard. BIDS and BCI say the new index is meant to give an independent, factory-level reading while official data catch up.

What it means for the development sector

Jobs and wages. Flat output, falling hires and almost no new machinery suggest manufacturing will not create many new jobs in the short term. Young people leaving school and training programmes will find fewer factory openings. This matters for TVET providers and NGO skills programmes that place graduates in industry.

Textile workers. A 20% fall in textile output and capacity use of 55% put spinning and weaving jobs at risk. These workers have received less attention than garment workers in this month's wage talks.

Garment wage talks. The garment sector grew slightly, but owners face higher energy and freight costs. Both sides in the Minimum Wage Board will be able to use parts of this survey. Workers can point to rising output in garments, while owners can point to costs.

Energy policy. Factories are paying more for generator fuel and LPG because grid power and gas are unreliable. That is also a pollution and health issue for workers and nearby communities. Climate and energy groups pushing for grid upgrades and renewable power have new evidence of what the shortfall costs.

Better data. The gap between the survey and official figures adds to concerns about the quality of national statistics. Researchers and donors using BBS figures for programme design should check them against independent sources where they can.

Limits of the evidence

This is the first round of a new survey, so there is no trend yet, only a comparison with 2025. The sample of 130 medium and large factories leaves out small, cottage and informal firms, which employ many manufacturing workers. The cost and sentiment figures come from what factories report. Devlens has relied on reporting by The Daily Star and The Business Standard and has not seen the full BIDS presentation.

The bottom line

Power and gas shortages are holding back Bangladesh's factories. Output has stalled, hiring has slowed, and investment in new machinery has almost stopped. Unless energy supply improves, manufacturing is unlikely to create the jobs the country needs, and textile workers face the most immediate risk.
